# Chapter 4: Linear Regression

## What I'm doing here

These are my notes for building a OLS linear regression model on the OULAD dataset.
The goal is to predict `avg_score` — a student's average assessment score across
a module — from things we could plausibly know about them: demographics, how many
credits they're taking, and how much they engage with the online course materials.

This follows Chapter 4 of Boehmke & Greenwell, but using tidymodels instead of
caret. The concepts are the same; the syntax is different.

As a reminder, this is a **predictive** model, not a causal one.
If `total_clicks` turns out to matter, that doesn't mean telling students to click
more would raise their scores. It means clicking could be correlated with something — motivation, time available, engagement — that does affect scores.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(skimr)
library(caret) # to examine nzv
library(corrr) # correlation check
library(rcompanion) # correlation check
library(DALEXtra) # explain models

set.seed(1234)
```

Without seed, the train/test split would be different every time
I run this code and my numbers wouldn't match what I wrote in my narrative.

## Data dictionary

Keeping this here for reference.

```
IDENTIFIERS
  id_student          Unique student identifier

COURSE CONTEXT
  code_module         Course module code (AAA-GGG, 7 modules)
  code_presentation   Presentation period (e.g., "2013J" = 2013 Fall)
  domain              STEM or Social Science (determined by code_module)

STUDENT DEMOGRAPHICS
  gender              M or F
  region              UK region of residence
  highest_education   Prior education level
  imd_band            Index of Multiple Deprivation band (0-10% most deprived)
  age_band            0-35, 35-55, or 55<=
  disability          Y/N

ENROLLMENT
  num_of_prev_attempts        Prior attempts at this module
  studied_credits             Credits enrolled this presentation
  date_registration           Days relative to module start (negative = early)
  date_unregistration         Days to withdrawal (NA if completed) - LEAKAGE
  module_presentation_length  Module length in days

ENGAGEMENT
  total_clicks        Total VLE clicks
  total_days_active   Distinct days with activity
  n_assessments       Assessments taken

ASSESSMENT PERFORMANCE
  avg_score           Average score (0-100) - TARGET
  min_score           Lowest score - LEAKAGE
  max_score           Highest score - LEAKAGE
  n_failed            Count of failed assessments - LEAKAGE
  avg_days_early      Average days submitted early (negative = late)

OUTCOME
  final_result        Pass / Distinction / Fail / Withdrawn
  wf                  Binary target for the classification version
```

## Loading and cleaning

A bunch of columns come in as character because of how missing values were
written in the source file. Coercing them to numeric so the recipe can work with
them.

```{r}
#| label: load

oulad_raw <- read_csv("oulad_clean.csv")
oulad <- oulad_raw %>%
  mutate(
    avg_score         = as.numeric(avg_score),
    avg_days_early    = as.numeric(avg_days_early),
    n_assessments     = as.numeric(n_assessments),
    total_clicks      = as.numeric(total_clicks),
    total_days_active = as.numeric(total_days_active),
    date_registration = as.numeric(date_registration)
  )

glimpse(oulad)
Sys.time()
```

This mutate happens **before** the split, and that's fine. Type coercion doesn't
learn anything from the data — turning `"52.5"` into `52.5` gives the same answer
no matter which rows are around it. Compare that to something like imputation,
which learns a median from the training rows and would leak if I did it out here.


## Looking at the data before I model anything

```{r}
#| label: skim
skim(oulad)

```

The `complete_rate` column is the interesting one. Several engagement variables
have real missingness — students who never touched the VLE don't have click
counts.

### How much of the target is missing?
These are students who never submitted an assessment, so they have no average
score. I can't train on them — the model needs to see the answer to learn.

```{r}
#| label: target-missing
oulad %>%
  summarise(
    n_rows             = n(),
    n_missing_target   = sum(is.na(avg_score)),
    pct_missing_target = mean(is.na(avg_score)) * 100
  )
```
